title: [MM][Mistral] Add compile support for Pixtral vision encoders
body:
## Purpose
Add `compile_mm_encoder` support for both Pixtral vision encoder implementations:

- `PixtralForConditionalGeneration`, including Mistral-format Mistral 3 models.
- The Hugging Face Pixtral encoder used by `Mistral3ForConditionalGeneration`.

The change applies `support_torch_compile` to the transformer blocks in both implementations and marks the token, rotary embedding, and packed-sequence dimensions as dynamic.

The feature remains gated behind `compile_mm_encoder`, which is disabled by default.

### Performance results
Note: the results are only about GPU kernel time. Total E2E runtime improves much less, even with Cuda graphs from #56277, because apply_hf_processor is the main bottleneck now.

Profiling was performed on an NVIDIA GB200 system using the same 16-image BF16 capture before and after enabling compilation. 
Total GPU kernel time decreased by **42%**, from **1173.6 ms to 676.8 ms**, corresponding to a **1.73x speedup**.

The improvement came from eliminating or fusing much of execution overhead:

| Kernel category | Before | After | Reduction |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| FlashAttention | 273 ms | 273 ms | 0% |
| GEMM | 272 ms | 272 ms | 0% |
| Elementwise operations | 368 ms | 11 ms | 97% |
| SiLU | 121 ms | 44 ms | 64% |
| Concat | 96 ms | 0.3 ms | >99% |


  ### CUDA-graph compatibility

  This work is complementary to #56277, which adds Pixtral encoder CUDA-graph support. It does not duplicate or modify that implementation.

  The CUDA-graph PR’s pixtral.py and mistral3.py changes apply cleanly over this change. Its packed encoder forwards continue to use the unchanged transformer interface. Encoder CUDA-graph capture also performs an eager warmup before capture,
  allowing the transformer blocks to compile first.

  A combined compile_mm_encoder=True plus cudagraph_mm_encoder=True integration test should be added once #56277 is merged.

## Test Plan
Exercise both encoder implementations with compilation enabled and disabled:

- Mistral-format `PixtralForConditionalGeneration`
- Hugging Face `Mistral3ForConditionalGeneration`

The test uses dummy weights and verifies that the compilation counter increases only when `compile_mm_encoder` is enabled.

  tests/compile/fullgraph/test_multimodal_compile.py \

4 passed, 4 deselected

title: [Bugfix][Quantization] Fix MXFP8 startup crash on layers below mm_mxfp8 shape limits
body:
## Purpose

`vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B --quantization mxfp8` dies in the profile run on a B200 with `AssertionError: mm_mxfp8 requires N >= 128, got N=32`. The layer is the GDN `in_proj_ba` (weight 32 x 1024). The larger Qwen3.5 sizes and Qwen3-Next have N=64 or N=96 there, so the whole family fails to start with online MXFP8.

`FlashInferCutlassMxfp8LinearKernel` and `FlashInferCutedslMxfp8LinearKernel` return `True` from `can_implement` for every layer. The `mm_mxfp8` shape limits (N >= 128, K >= 128, K % 32 == 0) are only asserts inside `apply_weights`, so on SM100 a layer below the limits is still selected instead of falling through to Marlin.

`Mxfp8LinearLayerConfig` gains `weight_shape` and the two kernels check the limits in `can_implement`. The compressed-tensors, INC and online MXFP8 schemes select the kernel in `create_weights` instead of `__init__`, the per-layer pattern `Fp8LinearMethod` already uses. ModelOpt already selects in `create_weights` since #49381, so there this PR only forwards the weight shape, including the BMM re-selection where the weight can be `[batch, N, K]`. No kernel code changes.

From @stecasta's review: on SM12x the CUTLASS kernel also rejects N % 32 != 0, and `MarlinMxfp8LinearKernel.can_implement` now rejects N <= 0, K <= 0 and K % 32 != 0.

## Test plan

```
pytest tests/kernels/quantization/test_mxfp8_kernel_selection.py tests/kernels/quantization/test_flashinfer_mxfp8_trtllm.py tests/quantization/test_modelopt.py
pytest tests/kernels/quantization/test_mxfp4_kernel_selection.py tests/model_executor/kernels/test_b12x_linear.py tests/kernels/test_minimax_m3_amd_ops.py tests/quantization/test_auto_round.py -k "mxfp8 or inc or selection or b12x or minimax"
pytest tests/kernels/quantization/test_marlin_tile_padding.py -k test_mxfp8_marlin_padded_round_trip  # GPU
```

On a B200 I ran `LLM("Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B", quantization="mxfp8")` on `main` and with this patch applied, then generated 8 tokens.

## Test result

The first two commands give 164 passed and 11 skipped on CPU, on the rebased branch (main 54020c3c3e). On an L4 and an RTX PRO 6000 (SM120), the third passes for all five shapes, including the new (32, 256), (96, 256) and (130, 256). `pre-commit run` is clean on the changed files. The B200 run below is from the original base d1922cb5a; the rebase changed no kernel code.

B200, vLLM 0.28.1rc1.dev49+gd1922cb5a, FlashInfer 0.6.17, CUDA 13.0:

| arm | startup | MXFP8 kernels selected | output for "The capital of France is" |
|---|---|---|---|
| `main` | fails in `profile_run` after 52 s: `AssertionError: mm_mxfp8 requires N >= 128, got N=32` | `FlashInferCutedslMxfp8LinearKernel` | none |
| this PR | ok | `FlashInferCutedslMxfp8LinearKernel`, `MarlinMxfp8LinearKernel` | ` Paris.` |

`in_proj_ba` is the only quantized linear in this model with N < 128, so it is the layer Marlin took (padded to N=64, the log shows the Marlin padding warning). Every other layer still gets the FlashInfer kernel.

## Notes

Developed with Claude Code. I reviewed every line and ran the tests myself.

@stecasta adapted this change for SM12x and measured a throughput gain on DGX Spark over all-Marlin MXFP8, see https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54223#issuecomment-5760441790.

Duplicate check: no open PR adds shape checks to any MXFP8 `can_implement`. #49381 landed and already moved the ModelOpt kernel selection into `create_weights`; this PR is rebased on it. #51808 adds an `activation_quant_key` argument to `init_mxfp8_linear_kernel`; I will rebase if it lands first. #52275 changes the TRT-LLM kernel in the same file and does not touch selection.

title: [Bugfix][Tool Parser] Migrate Granite to the streaming Parser Engine
body:
This PR started as a fix for Granite tool calls wrapped in surrounding text. At
@chaunceyjiang's request, it now **migrates the Granite parser to the streaming Parser
Engine** — which fixes the surrounding-text case and several streaming bugs as a side
effect.

## Why the engine work

Granite's tool-call format is the hard case for the engine: **one marker → a JSON array
of N tool calls, with no closing terminal** —
`<|tool_call|> [{"name":..,"arguments":{..}}, ...]`. Every other engine parser is
one-marker-one-call, so the engine needed a way to fan a single array into N calls.

## What's in each commit

1. **Engine** (`tool_call_body_array`): opt-in flag, **default off → zero change for
   existing parsers**. The fan-out happens at the event-generation layer, so the
   non-streaming path and all slot machinery are reused with no changes.
2. **Refactor**: share Inkling's JSON member-object scanner via `vllm/parser/utils.py`
   (behavior-preserving; that's why `inkling.py` is touched).
3. **Granite**: the parser itself — modeled on Inkling (JSON body + name-from-args), with
   an `arg_converter` to carve each element's `arguments`. Legacy parser deleted; scope
   limited to `granite` (3.0/3.1), leaving `granite-20b-fc` and `granite4` untouched.

## Notes for review (the non-obvious bits)

- The **marker transition emits no `TOOL_CALL_START`** — the array splitter emits
  START/END per element, because one marker = N calls.
- **No non-streaming changes**: both paths share the event pipeline, so the fan-out
  covers both.
- A **truncated (mid-element) stream** gets one synthetic `TOOL_CALL_END`; closed
  elements already emitted theirs (guarded in `finish()`).
- A **marker not followed by `[`** (malformed) reverts to content — no tool call.
- Granite **needs an `arg_converter`** because each element is a `{"name","arguments"}`
  wrapper; without it the wrapper would leak into the OpenAI `arguments` field.

## Test plan

**CPU (all green):**
- `pytest tests/tool_parsers/test_granite_tool_parser.py` — 25 passed (the 4 previously
  `xfail`'d cases — surrounding text ×2, streaming reconstruction, malformed streaming —
  now pass; markers removed).
- `pytest tests/parser/engine/test_granite.py` — 28 passed (arg-converter units,
  non-streaming, streaming chunk-invariance, self-validating replay).
- `pytest tests/parser/engine/ tests/tool_parsers/` — full regression green
  (`test_replay` / `test_delegating_replay` enforce the engine-parser registry;
  `test_inkling.py` confirms the refactor is behavior-preserving).
- `pre-commit run` — clean.

**GPU end-to-end** (real models served with `--tool-call-parser granite`; streaming +
non-streaming; single + parallel calls):
- **granite-3.1-2b** (`<tool_call>` text marker): all correct. Raw model output confirmed
  `<tool_call>[{"arguments":..,"name":..}, {...}]` — JSON array, `arguments` before
  `name`.
- **granite-3.0-2b** (`<|tool_call|>` single special token): parallel calls correct,
  streaming + non-streaming.

## AI assistance

This change was developed with AI assistance (Claude). I have reviewed every line, run the
tests above, and validated the behavior end-to-end on a GPU.

title: [KV Offload][FS] Opt-in per-block CRC32C checksums
body:
## Purpose
Implements item 1 of #54363. The FS tier catches a truncated block (short read) but not one whose bytes changed at the same size, e.g. bit rot; such a block is loaded as KV silently.

New tier option `checksum_blocks` (default `false`), using the xattr approach preferred in the #54363 discussion:

* **Store:** the block's CRC32C is set as xattr `user.vllm.kv_crc32c` on the temp file, before the rename.

* **Load:** verified after the read. A verification failure removes the file, fails the load with `EBADMSG` through the existing `num_succeeded` partial-keep path, and increments `vllm:kv_offload_tiering_checksum_failures`.

* **Backward compatible:** a block with no recorded checksum still loads, so the option can be enabled on an existing cache. For the same reason `FileMapper.fields` is not bumped, unlike the RFC text: the file contents do not change, so there is no cold start.

* **xattrs unavailable at `root_dir`:** the tier fails at startup (see the design decision below).

* Implemented in both `csrc/fs_io.cpp` (SSE4.2, table fallback) and the Python fallback in `fs/io.py`. With the option off, no CRC or xattr call is made and the metric is not registered.

`batch_store_block` / `batch_load_block` in `fs_io_C` gain a trailing `checksum` argument, so the extension must be rebuilt with this change.

Limitation: hardware CRC32C is x86-64 only. Other architectures, including ARM, use the table implementation (same value, slower); ARM hardware CRC can follow separately.

No open PR references #54363, and searches for `checksum kv offload`, `crc32c` and `xattr` find none in this area.

### Design decision to confirm

#54363 did not settle what checksum mode should do when xattrs are unavailable: fail, or disable itself with a warning. I chose to fail at startup, because a silent fallback hides that blocks are no longer verified. Is that acceptable?

## Test Plan

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/v1/kv_offload/ -q
pre-commit run --from-ref upstream/main --to-ref HEAD
pre-commit run mypy-3.12 --hook-stage manual --from-ref upstream/main --to-ref HEAD
```

New tests in `test_fs_tier.py`, on both I/O paths where applicable: same recorded value on both paths, corrupt data / corrupt record, legacy block still loads, xattr set before the rename, startup failure without xattrs, metric registered only when enabled.

## Test Result

* `tests/v1/kv_offload/`: 668 passed, 2 skipped (`test_fs_tier.py`: 56 passed, 12 new).
* pre-commit and `mypy-3.12`: passed.

### Cost when enabled

i7-14700F, ext4 on NVMe, `O_DIRECT`, `fs_io_C`, one thread, median per block:

| Block   | Store off → on (µs) | Load off → on (µs) | Device writes/block off / on | Device reads/block off / on |
| ------- | ------------------- | ------------------ | ---------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| 256 KiB | 84.2 → 107.3        | 180.1 → 214.2      | 2.10 / 2.12                  | 2.00 / 2.00                 |
| 1 MiB   | 207.2 → 300.4       | 275.8 → 393.5      | 8.16 / 8.13                  | 8.00 / 8.00                 |
| 4 MiB   | 679.3 → 1043.3      | 709.8 → 1090.1     | 32.35 / 32.39                | 32.00 / 32.00               |

Device I/O counts are effectively unchanged in this ext4/NVMe setup (the 4-byte value lives in the inode) and the xattr calls take under 1 µs. The added latency is the CRC32C pass, about 12 GB/s here.

## Notes

* No behavior change by default: `checksum_blocks` is off unless explicitly enabled, so no model evals were run. When enabled, a checksum failure turns a corrupted cache hit into a miss and recompute instead of returning the corrupted KV block.

* AI assistance (Claude) was used. I have reviewed every changed line and ran the tests above.

- Extend the NVFP4 emulation suite with eight dense-kernel cases covering an independent CPU reference, bias, zero blocks, graph replay and output lifetime.

title: [Metrics][KV Offload] Fill vllm:kv_offload_config_info with the CPU cache capacity
body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Purpose

GPU KV-cache capacity is observable. `num_gpu_blocks` and `kv_cache_size_tokens`
are labels on `vllm:cache_config_info`. The CPU offload tier exports only usage
(`vllm:kv_offload_cpu_cache_usage_perc` and the read/write variants) and no
capacity. The size is not recoverable externally either, because it depends on
`blocks_per_chunk`, page alignment, and whether a replicated layout deduplicates
the per-worker copies. All three are connector-internal.

This PR fills `vllm:kv_offload_config_info` with the CPU cache facts. The gauge,
the label rendering and the emission call come from #56867, the generic
config-info PR. The CPU side adds four labels:

| Label | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `cpu_num_chunks` | Chunk slots in the tier. Chunks, not GPU blocks. |
| `cpu_blocks_per_chunk` | GPU blocks in one chunk: the chunk-to-block conversion factor. |
| `cpu_kv_bytes_per_chunk` | Page-aligned bytes of one chunk. With `cpu_num_chunks` it gives the exact size of the tier in bytes. |
| `cpu_capacity_tokens_at_max_len` | Upper bound on the KV tokens the tier holds, over the request lengths up to `max_model_len`. |

No name carries a tier index, so a CPU fact reads the same under
`CPUOffloadingSpec` and under `TieringOffloadingSpec`. The gauge is per engine.
Sum across the `engine` label for the instance total. The Info shape is the
extensible container the reviewers of #49307 asked for.

### `capacity_tokens_at_max_len`

The tier is content-addressed (`OffloadKey = block_hash + group_idx`), so there is
no per-request allocation to divide by, and no analogue of the GPU
`max_concurrency`. The capacity in tokens therefore depends on the request
length, and one model can spend its slots very differently at 1k tokens and at
32k tokens. The label reports the largest value the tier reaches over the lengths
the code measures:

```
chunks_per_request(T) = sum over groups of min(cdiv(T, tokens_per_chunk), cap)
capacity(T)           = num_chunks * T // chunks_per_request(T)
label                 = max over candidate T of capacity(T)
```

Both `tokens_per_chunk` and `cap` are per group. `tokens_per_chunk` is
`blocks_per_chunk * tokens_per_block` of that group. `cap` is the chunks of that
group the tier keeps for one request: `None` for attention that reaches back
without a bound, `cdiv(window, tokens_per_chunk)` for a sliding window, and 1 for
Mamba. A capped group holds a fixed number of chunks however long the request
grows, so a longer request spreads that fixed cost over more tokens.

Two values cross the `OffloadingConfig` boundary for this:
`OffloadingGroupConfig.sliding_window_size_in_chunks`, which reads the bound the
scheduler already computes with `get_sliding_window_size_in_chunks`, and
`OffloadingModelConfig.max_model_len`.

`None` covers three cases where no request length is defined: a `max_model_len`
of 0, no KV cache group at all, and a group whose block spans no tokens. Zero
chunks reports `0`, not `None`, because zero slots hold exactly zero tokens.

`num_chunks * kv_bytes_per_chunk` stays exact for every model, because every slot
is the same byte size. The tier is uniform in bytes and non-uniform in tokens.

### Why this estimate

The GPU side answers the same question in the same three steps.
`get_kv_cache_capacity` (`kv_cache_utils.py:2291`) builds `kv_cache_size_tokens`
like this:

```
num_blocks_per_request = sum over groups of cdiv(max_memory_usage_bytes, page_size_bytes)
max_concurrency        = num_blocks / num_blocks_per_request
kv_cache_size_tokens   = int(max_concurrency * max_model_len)
```

Sum the per-request cost over the groups, divide the pool by that sum, multiply by
the request length. The formula above does the same, with chunks in place of blocks.

The per-group cap matches too. `SlidingWindowSpec.max_memory_usage_bytes` calls
`max_admission_blocks_per_request`, which bounds a windowed group by its window
(`kv_cache_interface.py:716`). `MambaSpec.max_memory_usage_bytes` charges one page
for each request in the default cache mode (`kv_cache_interface.py:922`). So `cap`
states on the tier what the GPU pool already states on itself.

Both numbers report an upper bound. `kv_cache_size_tokens` assumes that every
request reaches `max_model_len`, and that every block holds data. The label bounds
the tier the same way, over the request lengths up to `max_model_len`. So an
operator reads the two side by side, and asks one question of both: how much
context fits at most.

### Worked examples

Every number below comes from the shipped `_capacity_tokens_at_max_len`. `held` is
`min(cdiv(T, tokens_per_chunk), cap)`, the chunks one request keeps in that group.

**Qwen3-8B**, TP 2, 1 full attention group, `tokens_per_chunk` 256, 4500 slots,
`max_model_len` 36864:

| Groups | cap | cdiv(36864, 256) | held | subtotal |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 full | None | 144 | 144 | 144 |

`4500 * 36864 // 144 = 1152000`. One uncapped group gives the same value at every
full chunk, because the request length and the chunk count grow together.

**gemma-3-27b-it**, TP 2, 1 full group and 6 sliding-window groups, window 1024
tokens, so `cap` is 4 chunks. `tokens_per_chunk` 256, 4000 slots, `max_model_len`
36864:

| Groups | cap | cdiv(36864, 256) | held | subtotal |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 full | None | 144 | 144 | 144 |
| 6 SWA | 4 | 144 | 4 | 24 |

`chunks_per_request = 168`, and `4000 * 36864 // 168 = 877714`. The 6 windowed
groups cost 24 chunks together, less than the single full group.

**granite-4.0-h-small**, TP 2, 1 full group and 9 Mamba groups, `tokens_per_chunk`
528, 8000 slots, `max_model_len` 36864. The peak sits at T 36432, the last full
chunk before `max_model_len`:

| Groups | cap | cdiv(36432, 528) | held | subtotal |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 full | None | 69 | 69 | 69 |
| 9 Mamba | 1 | 69 | 1 | 9 |

`chunks_per_request = 78`, and `8000 * 36432 // 78 = 3736615`. Nine Mamba groups
cost 9 chunks however long the request runs.

**A hybrid with one group of each kind**, `tokens_per_chunk` 256, 4000 slots,
`max_model_len` 36864, window 1024 tokens:

| Groups | cap | cdiv(36864, 256) | held | subtotal |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 full | None | 144 | 144 | 144 |
| 1 SWA | 4 | 144 | 4 | 4 |
| 1 Mamba | 1 | 144 | 1 | 1 |

`chunks_per_request = 149`, and `4000 * 36864 // 149 = 989637`. Charge all three
groups the growing term and the answer drops to 341333, a factor of 2.9. The caps
carry most of the number on a hybrid model.

**On the candidate lengths.** `chunks_per_request` is a step function of T, and it
never falls, so the capacity rises between two steps and drops at each step. Every
peak therefore sits at the last length before a step, which is a multiple of the
`tokens_per_chunk` of a group. The code measures one such length for each distinct
value, plus `max_model_len` for the final partial chunk. That set holds the true
peak when every group shares one `tokens_per_chunk`, which covers all four cases
above. When the values differ, as in a mix of MLA and SWA, the set can understate
the peak by a small amount. The label is an estimate, so that difference does not
change how an operator reads it.

### Relation to #56867, #49307 and #51615

**#56867** adds `vllm:kv_offload_config_info` and the mechanism that fills it, with
no real value behind it. This PR supplies the CPU values, so #56867 must land first.

**#49307 (@yanburman)** became this same metric after review (@orozery: bundle
static tier information into one Info metric following `vllm:cache_config_info`),
emitted once at engine startup. That needed a new public `get_config_info()`
connector API, an `EngineCoreReadyResponse` field, a runtime-populated
`KVTransferConfig` side-channel and a `record_config_info()` chain. All of those
edit code outside `kv_offload/` and `offloading/`, which reviewers objected to.
**#51615 (@nilig, draft)** emits `vllm:kv_offload_cpu_capacity_tokens` through the
existing connector-stats path.

This PR takes the metric shape of #49307 and the emission mechanism of #51615. The
cost is that the metric is absent (no series, never `0`) until the first scheduler
step.

## Test Plan

- **Unit tests** — 20 new tests, over four sections of the change.

    - **The capacity arithmetic** — `_chunks_per_request` and
      `_capacity_tokens_at_max_len` take plain arguments, so the tests cover the
      four model shapes above, the sawtooth peak, the per-group cap, and every
      case where the token scale is not known.
    - **The tier sizing** — the labels of a real `CPUOffloadingSpec` report the
      numbers the spec resolved, under tensor parallel, under a replicated
      layout, and with a second group that shares the slots.
    - **The config boundary** — `build_offloading_config` fills the two new
      fields, `sliding_window_size_in_chunks` on the group and `max_model_len` on
      the model.
    - **The tiering pass-through** — the primary tier keeps the four labels
      unprefixed, the tiering spec gives it the chunk size and the configuration,
      and the tiering spec declares exactly the names the manager fills.

    Files: `tests/v1/kv_offload/cpu/test_capacity.py` is new and holds 6.
    `tests/v1/kv_offload/test_factory.py` holds 11,
    `tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/offloading_connector/test_config.py` holds 2, and
    `tests/v1/kv_offload/cpu/test_manager.py` holds 1.
    `tests/v1/kv_offload/tiering/test_tiering_offloading.py` gains no test. Its
    drift guard now pins the four CPU names next to the secondary tier names.

    ```bash
    # every test file this PR changes or adds, plus the two shared metric files
    .venv/bin/python -m pytest \
      tests/v1/kv_offload/test_factory.py \
      tests/v1/kv_offload/cpu/test_capacity.py \
      tests/v1/kv_offload/cpu/test_manager.py \
      tests/v1/kv_offload/tiering/test_tiering_offloading.py \
      tests/v1/kv_offload/tiering/test_metrics.py \
      tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/offloading_connector/test_config.py \
      tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/offloading_connector/test_metrics.py -q

    # the scope of the H200 CI job, minus the nixl/moriio/bidirectional suites.
    # 7 of them import ray, which is not installed locally
    .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/v1/kv_offload tests/v1/kv_connector/unit -q \
      --ignore-glob='*moriio*' --ignore-glob='*nixl*' --ignore-glob='*bidirectional*' \
      --continue-on-collection-errors
    ```

- **Lint** — `pre-commit run --all-files` and
  `pre-commit run mypy-3.12 --all-files --hook-stage manual`, as CI runs it.

- **Documentation** — `docs/features/kv_offloading_usage.md` gains an "Info Metric
  Labels" section, which documents the four labels and the secondary-tier prefix.

- **Model evaluations: not applicable.** Metrics only. The two hooks return static
  values that the scheduler reads once, and only `_build_config_info` reads the new
  capacity functions. The PR touches no scheduling, no KV-cache placement, no
  transfer behavior and no model output.

- **GPU run** — one H100 80GB, one engine, `facebook/opt-125m` at
  `--max-model-len 2048`, `cpu_bytes_to_use` of 4 GiB, `blocks_per_chunk` of 200, and
  one `fs` secondary tier. The run scrapes `/metrics` after two completion requests.

- **Data-parallel run** — two H100 80GB, `--data-parallel-size 2`, `cpu_bytes_to_use`
  of 2 GiB, and no secondary tier. Both engines report the four labels under a separate
  `engine` value. The Test Result section gives the numbers.

- **Not verified.** A real hybrid Mamba model stays untested. The development
  environment is macOS without CUDA, so the H200 job covers the worker path and
  `SharedOffloadRegion`.

## Test Result

**The seven test files above**, at the branch tip: `301 passed, 1 skipped`.

`test_capacity.py` pins `capacity_tokens_at_max_len` for Qwen3-8B, gemma-3-27b-it and
granite-4.0-h-small, so the arithmetic is covered there and not repeated here.

**Single engine**, one H100 80GB, `facebook/opt-125m` at `--max-model-len 2048`,
`cpu_bytes_to_use` of 4 GiB, `blocks_per_chunk` of 200, and one `fs` secondary tier:
`cpu_blocks_per_chunk="200"`, `cpu_kv_bytes_per_chunk="117964800"`,
`cpu_num_chunks="36"` and `cpu_capacity_tokens_at_max_len="73728"`. A 200-block chunk
holds 3200 tokens, which is more than `max_model_len`, so the label reports the 73728
usable tokens and not the 115200 that the raw slot count suggests.

**Two engines**, two H100 80GB, `--data-parallel-size 2`, `cpu_bytes_to_use` of 2 GiB
and `blocks_per_chunk` of 4: both engines report `cpu_num_chunks="910"` and
`cpu_capacity_tokens_at_max_len="58240"` under a separate `engine` label. `world_size`
excludes the data-parallel size, so each engine sizes its own tier from the full
`cpu_bytes_to_use`, which makes the setting per engine and not per instance.

**The wider CI scope**, the second command above:
`81 failed, 1634 passed, 28 skipped, 4 errors`. Every failure comes from
`tests/v1/kv_offload/cpu/test_gpu_worker.py` or
`tests/v1/kv_offload/cpu/test_shared_offload_region.py`, which need CUDA and
`/dev/shm`. The macOS development environment gives neither. The 4 errors stop the
collection of the mooncake test modules, because the installed `huggingface_hub`
no longer exports `httpx`. That is why the run needs
`--continue-on-collection-errors`.

The same command on the #56867 tip gave `76 failed, 1399 passed, 26 skipped,
4 errors`. That measurement predates the last rebase of this branch, so read it as
a record of the failure class, not as a count to subtract. Both runs fail in the
same two files.

## AI assistance

Developed with AI assistance (Claude Code): the test suite, the capacity
derivation and its brute-force checks, and this description. The submitter
reviewed all code and reasoning line by line, and can defend the design and its
trade-offs.

title: [Bugfix][Attention] Fix FA4 FP8 descale strides for singleton KV heads
body:
## Purpose

Fix a FlashAttention 4 FP8 KV-cache crash when a per-tensor Q/K/V scale is expanded to a descale tensor with a non-unit head stride:

```text
Expected strides[leading_dim] == 1, but got 0
```

This was encountered in a Nemotron-H deployment with two total KV heads and TP=2 on B200 (vLLM 0.29.0). Each rank has one KV head. At batch size 1, `scalar.expand(1, 1)` has strides `(0, 0)` but PyTorch considers it contiguous, so `.contiguous()` can leave the incompatible stride unchanged. FA4 converts descales to CuTe tensors with `leading_dim=1`.

Materialize only 2-D FA4 descales whose head stride is not one using `clone(memory_format=torch.contiguous_format)`. Preserve compatible inputs and the existing non-FP8 behavior. This copies the small scale tensors, not the KV cache.

## Test Plan

Add a CPU regression suite that calls the production `flash_attn_varlen_func` and replaces only the downstream CuTe kernel entry point. It verifies the forwarded descale layout, values, and reuse of compatible inputs across:

- batch sizes 1 and 3;
- one and two local KV heads;
- scalar-expanded, per-head-expanded, and absent descales;
- FP8 e4m3, FP8 e5m2, and BF16 inputs.

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest --noconftest tests/kernels/attention/test_flash_attn_interface.py -q
pre-commit run --files vllm/vllm_flash_attn/flash_attn_interface.py tests/kernels/attention/test_flash_attn_interface.py
```

The sibling kernel suite requires the CUDA package initializer. This test loads the Python wrapper directly so it can also run on a CPU-only machine. The existing attention-kernel CI glob includes the new file.

## Test Result

Base: `a9f07d0bc59604d3979ba0f232469f4a80eb8175` (2026-09-23 main).
Local environment: macOS arm64, Python 3.13.9, PyTorch 2.13.0, pytest 9.1.1.

- Regression suite on unmodified main: **8 failed, 28 passed**. Failures are FP8 scalar-expanded descales reaching the kernel boundary with head stride zero.
- Same suite after the fix: **36 passed**. Both runs emitted a warning that optional NumPy was not installed.
- All applicable pre-commit hooks passed, including Ruff, mypy 3.10, and CI test tethering.
- Manual `mypy-3.12` hook passed.
- `py_compile` on both changed files and `git diff --check` passed.

No B200 is currently available, so this branch has not been tested with the real FA4 kernel, CUDA graphs, or an end-to-end model on current main. The CPU test checks the wrapper contract, not attention numerics or GPU performance.

Historical deployment validation (v0.29.0, earlier version of this fix): a TP=2 B200 serving run completed 80 multilingual requests with zero API failures. This was a serving smoke test, not a scored accuracy evaluation or a controlled performance comparison. Three requests exhausted the 4096-token budget with no final content. These results do not replace current-main GPU validation.

## Duplicate-work check

Checked current main and open/closed PRs using `descale`, `FA4 stride`, `descale stride`, `leading_dim`, and the error message.

- #51363 forwards FP8 descales through FA4; it does not normalize their strides.
- #40737 canonicalizes KV-cache tensor strides, not descale tensors.
- Open #53175, #48156, and #54705 cover other FA4/FP8 functionality and do not implement this fix.

## AI assistance

OpenAI Codex assisted with investigation, implementation, and tests. The human submitter is responsible for reviewing the diff and validation evidence.

title: [Bugfix][Core] Hash every multimodal input in a block finished by generation
body:
## Purpose

`request_block_hasher` starts the multimodal scan at the **last** mm input whenever it is not hashing from token 0:

```python
# vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_utils.py
curr_mm_idx = 0
if start_token_idx > 0:
    # Set curr_mm_idx = -1 to indicate the last mm input.
    # Note that since we reach to this branch only when the block is
    # completed with generated tokens, we only need to consider the
    # last mm input.
    curr_mm_idx = -1
```

The premise in that comment does not hold. The block completed by generated tokens is the same block that held the tail of the prompt, and that block can overlap **more than one** mm input — the end of the second-to-last one, plus a last one shorter than the block. Starting at the last one drops the others from the block's extra keys.

So the block hash depends on *when* it was computed. With `block_size=16` and mm inputs at `(offset=17, length=2)` and `(offset=20, length=2)`, the extra keys for the block spanning tokens 16..31 are:

| how the block was hashed | extra keys |
|---|---|
| in the same pass as block 0 (prompt completed it) | `(('mm_first', 1), ('mm_second', 4))` |
| in a later pass (generation completed it) | `(('mm_second', 4),)` |

Two consequences:

**1. Same prefix, two different hashes.** The block is written to the prefix cache under one key and looked up under another.

**2. Different prefixes, same hash.** Two requests whose only difference is the dropped mm input produce the *same* block hash, so one can be served prefix-cache KV that was computed for a different image:

```
A: mm inputs ["mm_cat",   "mm_shared"]  ->  block 1 hash  X
B: mm inputs ["mm_dog",   "mm_shared"]  ->  block 1 hash  X     # collision
```

The one-shot path keeps these distinct, so this only bites once the block has been completed by generation — i.e. after the first decode steps of a request whose prompt does not end on a block boundary and whose last partial block holds two mm inputs.

`vllm/v1/core/block_pool.py` builds the `BlockStored` event's extra keys for the partial block with the same `-1 if block_start > 0 else 0`, so external KV-cache consumers were handed the same truncated key set.

## Changes

- `kv_cache_utils.py`: scan from the first mm input (`curr_mm_idx = 0`) in `request_block_hasher`.
- `block_pool.py`: same, for the `BlockStored` partial-block event.

**This is not a hot-path cost.** `_gen_mm_extra_hash_keys` already returns immediately when every mm input ends at or before `start_token_idx`:

```python
last_pos = mm_features[-1].mm_position
if last_pos.offset + last_pos.length <= start_token_idx:
    return extra_keys, start_mm_idx
```

which is the steady state during decode. Only the single block that still straddles the prompt tail walks the list, and that walk is bounded by the number of mm inputs on the request.

`_gen_mm_extra_hash_keys` keeps its negative-`start_mm_idx` support; after this change nothing passes a negative value, so it can be dropped too if you would rather not leave the branch around — I left it out of this diff to keep the change to the bug.

## Test

title: [Feature][Mamba] Batched two-phase grouped prefill execution for hybrid GDN/Mamba (+7.58x)
body:
## Purpose

Implements RFC #55697.

Part 3 of 3 for Application-Directed Mamba Prefix Checkpointing (depends on PR #55873 and PR #55875).

In hybrid GDN/Mamba models (such as Qwen3.5 35B-A3B), prefill batches containing shared prefixes (1 common Producer prompt + N distinct Consumer queries) previously required either sequential per-request execution or full prompt recomputation due to state recurrence.

This PR introduces batched two-phase grouped prefill execution in the worker and GDN layer:
- **Two-Phase Kernel Execution**: Splits the grouped prefill forward into batched Producer and Consumer phases. In Phase 1, all Producers run in a single packed kernel invocation and populate shared checkpoint state rows. In Phase 2, Consumers read the shared checkpoint rows (`index_select`), copy them to private destination slots (`index_copy_`), and compute suffixes concurrently in a second packed kernel invocation.
- **Attention Metadata Builder**: Automatically constructs `prefix_producer_ranges`, `consumer_ranges`, `consumer_shared_state_sources`, and `private_final_state_destination` to dispatch requests into packed phases.
- **Microbenchmark & Unit Tests**: Validates numerical equivalence against the sequential baseline and provides a reproducible benchmark demonstrating up to **7.58x speedup**.

## Microbenchmark Results (NVIDIA L40S, PyTorch 2.11.0+cu130)

Measured on an NVIDIA L40S GPU using `benchmarks/kernels/benchmark_grouped_gdn_prefill.py`:

| Workload (Producers, Consumers) | Tokens | Legacy Serial (us) | Batched Phased (us) | Speedup | P10 ~ P90 (us) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1P + 1C** (single candidate) | 576 | 2,146.41 | **1,548.13** | **1.39x** | 1,534 ~ 1,562 |
| **1P + 2C** | 640 | 2,876.00 | **1,546.33** | **1.86x** | 1,532 ~ 1,569 |
| **1P + 4C** | 768 | 4,245.61 | **1,545.72** | **2.75x** | 1,532 ~ 1,565 |
| **1P + 8C** (typical batch) | 1,024 | 7,055.63 | **1,582.38** | **4.46x** | 1,569 ~ 1,594 |
| **1P + 16C** (wide candidate batch) | 1,536 | 12,698.95 | **1,674.81** | **7.58x** | 1,660 ~ 1,716 |

### Performance Highlights:
- **Near-Flat Latency ($O(N) \to O(1)$)**: As consumers increase from 1 to 16, latency only increases from 1.54ms to 1.67ms (+8.4%), whereas serial execution scales linearly up to 12.7ms.
- **Substantial Throughput Gains**: At 16 consumers, latency drops by **86.8%**, yielding a **7.58x speedup**.

## Duplicate-work Check

- PR #55260 and #54612 optimize GDN decode-path kernels for MRV2/MTP, not prefill grouping.
- PR #54093 targets generic conv1d refactor.
- PR #42524 targets partial-group caching for PD disaggregation, not batched phased prefill execution.

### Relation to PR #53614 (Kimi-K3 Internal Checkpoints in v0.30.0)
- **PR #53614 (Kimi-K3)** introduces *model-internal* checkpoint extraction specific to the FlashKDA backend, heuristically exporting the last full-block state during speculative decoding without application-level semantic awareness. It cannot respect multimodal boundaries in 1-to-N structured prompts.
- **This PR (Application-Directed)** introduces *application-directed* checkpoint coordination across concurrent requests:
  1. Semantic boundaries are declared explicitly by the application prompt (`<|mamba_checkpoint|>`), perfectly preserving atomic multimodal image spans.
  2. Implements a global dependency state machine (`BlockPool` unready locking, same-step producer-consumer block inheritance, and ready state wakeup).
  3. Fully orthogonal and complementary to PR #53614, providing a general-purpose solution for hybrid GDN/Mamba architectures (e.g. Qwen3.5, Nemotron-4).

## Test Plan

- Kernel split equivalence test:
  `pytest tests/kernels/mamba/test_gdn_forward_core_split.py -v`
- Metadata builder test:
  `pytest tests/v1/attention/test_gdn_metadata_builder.py -k "test_grouped_metadata" -v`
- CPU GDN ops alignment test:
  `pytest tests/kernels/mamba/cpu/test_cpu_gdn_ops.py -v`
- Benchmark verification:
  `python -m benchmarks.kernels.benchmark_grouped_gdn_prefill --num-producers 1 --num-consumers 1 2 4 8 16`

title: [XPU] Wire up SYCL apply_rotary_emb kernel in ApplyRotaryEmb
body:
## Purpose

  `ApplyRotaryEmb.forward_cuda` imports `vllm.vllm_flash_attn.layers.rotary`, a CUDA-only
  module, so there is no `forward_xpu` override and every XPU call falls back to the CustomOp
  default `forward_native` (~8 elementwise kernels). `vllm_xpu_kernels` — already a pinned
  dependency (`requirements/xpu.txt`) — ships a SYCL `apply_rotary_emb` kernel that vLLM never
  calls. This adds an 11-line `forward_xpu` wiring it up, following the same per-backend pattern
  already used by `forward_cuda`/`forward_hip` in this class.


  ## Test Plan

  `pytest tests/kernels/core/test_apply_rotary_emb.py -v` on XPU hardware — 3 new XPU-gated
  cases (text / GPT-J interleaved / partial-rotary) comparing `forward_xpu` against
  `forward_native` bit-exact (`atol=0, rtol=0`).

  Additional correctness sweep across 12 shapes (vision + text, both RoPE styles, partial
  rotary), calling the real `forward_xpu`/CustomOp dispatch path (not the raw kernel).

  End-to-end check on GLM-4.1V-9B-Thinking (vision-heavy multimodal, eager mode, 4 images @
  1024px, 5 iterations), comparing wall-clock and output text SHA-256 before/after.

  ## Test Result

  `test_apply_rotary_emb.py`: 3 new cases pass; 4 pre-existing CUDA-only dispatch tests correctly
  skip on XPU.

  12-shape correctness sweep: maxerr 0.0 in all 12 cases.

  GLM-4.1V-9B-Thinking E2E: median latency 2.5414s -> 2.4794s (1.025x). Output text SHA-256
  identical between unpatched and patched arms across all 5 iterations — no behavior change
  beyond speed. RoPE is a small fraction of this model's device time, so the wall-clock win here
  is modest; the kernel-level win (measured separately, not included in this PR) is larger and
  should generalize better on RoPE-heavier models.

title: [Bugfix][ROCm] Fix startup OOM in AITER MLA FP8 prefill workspace sizing
body:
## Purpose

Fixes a startup OOM on Kimi K2.5 (or similar) when using the AITER ASM MLA prefill kernel, caused by overly pessimistic bounds on the size of the required persistent metadata buffers. These sizes were subsequently passed to the workspace manager which triggered the OOM.

**Triggered by**: The AITER bump to v0.1.22post1 picked up ROCm/aiter#3606 which slightly changed the logic for workspace sizing. 

**Long term fix in AITER**: https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/5759

### Why

For causal FP8 MLA the AITER backend uses a persistent kernel. It needs buffers to hold the work items to be completed by each work group. The metadata scheduler is responsible for sizing these buffers so that they are sufficiently large to handle any requests that might come in.  

The MLA metadata scheduler now emits a very loose bound. The bound is based on the assumption that every request can use max_qlen query tokens. (The actual upper bound is that the sum of query tokens equals max_num_batched_tokens). If one uses these to size the logits/attn_lse partial buffers we get huge KV reservations:

| max_num_batched_tokens | before aiter#3606 | after aiter#3606 (OOM) | this PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8192  | 1.88 GiB | 64.03 GiB  | 2.56 GiB |
| 16384 | 3.75 GiB | 128.03 GiB | 2.62 GiB |

**Short term fix**: Size with assumption that the total query tokens is bounded by the token budget.

**Long term fix**: AITER should give us this budget-aware max buffer size. Ticket: https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/issues/5729

title: [Bugfix][Weight Transfer] Preserve tied parameter names in ModuleSource
body:
## Purpose

Native weight sync can finish successfully while leaving a pipeline stage's output head on the previous weights. I reproduced this with a tied Hugging Face Qwen3-0.6B trainer and TP2/PP2 inference: `/weight_info` reported B, but both last-stage `lm_head` shards still matched A. Other inspected parameters matched B, and fixed-prompt logprobs differed from a fresh B engine by up to 2.0646.

`ModuleSource` currently uses the default `named_parameters()` iterator, which omits tied names. The trainer shares its input embedding and output head, but inference can need those names on different pipeline stages. Preserve all parameter names in both metadata and iteration, and document the extra alias materialization/transfer cost.

This addresses the native weight-sync parallelism work in #31848. I checked the existing source/alias reports and related PRs; #53541 adds single-inference-GPU transfer tests, while this fixes the built-in trainer source's missing parameter name. The checkpoint-aware untying behavior from #51665 remains necessary to respect explicit output heads.

## Test Plan

- Extend the existing `TestModuleSource` suite for tied Parameter names and repeated module aliases across two updates.
- Compare real native NCCL A→B→A updates with fresh engines using the same model, topology, prompts and inference settings. Inspect each rank's parameter shards and fixed-prompt/generated-token logprobs.
- Exercise both padded and unpadded tied/retied embedding layers through the real layerwise reload lifecycle, with split and combined loading.

## Test Result

- `tests/distributed/test_weight_transfer.py`: **73 passed, 18 skipped** with GPUs hidden; CUDA stayed uninitialized. The two new regression cases both fail against the unchanged base.
- Existing pre-commit hooks passed for all three changed files.
- CPU layerwise reload: eight configurations, two updates each, passed.
- Unpatched TP2/PP2 baseline: last-stage head stays on A after updating to B; max fixed-prompt logprob error **2.0645949840545654**. Initial A and restored A match their cold control exactly. Greedy IDs happen to match in this two-prompt example.
- Patched TP2/PP2 packed and TP2/PP1 unpacked: A→B→A matches the corresponding cold engines exactly for every inspected full parameter shard, continuation token ID and captured logprob entry. Maximum logprob error is **0.0**. Worker PIDs and inspected storage pointers stay unchanged; PP1 embedding/head sharing is preserved.

[Reproduction commands, frozen scripts and raw results](https://gist.github.com/JiataiWang/1e8362e42423d3c306f31af0dcdb9d83).

The model runs use BF16, eager FA2 and batch-invariant execution on A100s, with the same deterministic NCCL settings on trainer and workers. The local environment reuses official precompiled extensions from `2a02f6efe`; Python source is based on `fa1b3b19`. This is validation of the exercised paths, not an exact-source native rebuild or a performance benchmark.

AI assistance: Codex helped investigate, implement and test this change.

title: [ROCm][AITER] Add GDN long-prefill split-QKV fast path
body:
## Motivation

ROCm/aiter#4299 adds a channel-last HIP path for `causal_conv1d_fwd_split_qkv`, which can consume Qwen3.5's contiguous `[T, D]` projection through its logical `[D, T]` transpose without materializing a copy.

vLLM already fuses its packed post-conv split, normalization, and gating, so dispatching the AITER op unconditionally regresses short prompts. This change uses the AITER path only for long BF16 Qwen3.5 GDN prefills where it is faster, and retains the existing Triton/FLA path everywhere else.

A search of open vLLM PRs/issues did not find another change implementing this Qwen3.5 GDN channel-last split-QKV fast path.

## Summary

- Probe for AITER's optional GDN prefill split-QKV op and gracefully fall back with older AITER builds.
- Route non-interleaved Qwen3.5 BF16 prefills with at least 8192 tokens and width-4 convolution through the AITER channel-last kernel.
- Add a fused Triton postprocessor that normalizes AITER's split Q/K outputs in place and computes GDN gating in the same launch; V is already in its final contiguous layout.
- Precompute block-64 causal-conv metadata on the CPU to avoid a device-to-host synchronization at dispatch time while preserving block-8 metadata for the existing path.
- Cover variable-length inputs, initial states, the vLLM null cache slot, long production-shaped inputs, and split-output postprocessing.

## AITER dependency

- Required feature: ROCm/aiter#4299, now merged (`a96ee7b6e3c2688b099d6e32ec662bce8886efa7`).
- End-to-end validation pin: AITER main `d19f33251400bbc21a3a49cc8db421f918716b93`.
- AITER at this revision requires FlyDSL >= 0.2.4; the benchmark runtime pins FlyDSL 0.2.4.
- Older AITER builds remain supported through the importability probe and use the existing Triton/FLA fallback.

## Test plan

- [x] `pytest -q tests/kernels/test_fused_gdn_post_conv.py` — 68 passed
- [x] `pytest -q tests/kernels/mamba/test_aiter_gdn_prefill.py` — 2 passed
- [x] `pytest -q tests/v1/attention/test_gdn_metadata_builder.py` — 9 passed
- [x] AITER `test_causal_conv1d_prefill_split_qkv.py -k hip_channel_last` — 11 passed
- [x] `torch.compile(..., fullgraph=True)` smoke test for split-QKV postprocessing
- [x] Ruff format/check, forbidden-import, torch-cuda-call, typos, and diff checks
- [x] Qwen3.5-35B-A3B TP4 end-to-end serving A/B on MI308X/gfx942
- [x] Full 1319-question GSM8K, 5-shot, concurrency 256

Unit tests used `vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:v0.24.0`. End-to-end tests used that image with FlyDSL 0.2.4, vLLM baseline `afc94523c` vs PR `758e13f15`, and the same AITER `d19f332514` on both sides.

## Serve command

Hardware: 4x AMD Instinct MI308X (gfx942), ROCm driver 6.16.13. Model: local BF16 `Qwen3.5-35B-A3B`.

```bash
HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1,2,3 VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1 vllm serve /models/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B   --served-model-name Qwen3.5-35B-A3B   --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000   --tensor-parallel-size 4   --trust-remote-code   --dtype bfloat16   --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85   --max-model-len 32768   --max-num-seqs 256   --max-num-batched-tokens 32768
```

## End-to-end performance

Each random workload was warmed up and then run three times with `temperature=0`, `ignore_eos=true`, fixed seed 20260727, and the same four GPUs. Values below are medians across the three runs. `ISL/OSL` are tokens per request.

| Workload | Baseline total tok/s | PR total tok/s | Baseline median TTFT | PR median TTFT | Baseline p99 TTFT | PR p99 TTFT |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| ISL 4096 / OSL 1 / C1 / 8 prompts (fallback control) | 25,197.1 | 25,259.8 (+0.25%) | 161.37 ms | 161.64 ms (-0.17%) | 167.80 ms | 170.33 ms |
| ISL 8192 / OSL 1 / C1 / 8 prompts (dispatch threshold) | 29,045.6 | 29,186.3 (+0.48%) | 283.37 ms | 280.48 ms (+1.03%) | 293.99 ms | 291.89 ms |
| ISL 16384 / OSL 1 / C1 / 4 prompts (long prefill) | 25,250.4 | 25,486.3 (+0.93%) | 648.12 ms | 643.43 ms (+0.73%) | 662.01 ms | 653.29 ms |
| ISL 8192 / OSL 128 / C256 / 256 prompts (loaded serving) | 25,113.6 | 26,989.7 (+7.47%) | 44.034 s | 40.399 s (+8.25%) | 78.858 s | 72.458 s |

For the loaded workload, request throughput improved from 3.018 to 3.244 req/s (+7.47%), and mean TPOT improved from 323.73 to 306.22 ms (-5.41%). All runs completed with zero failed requests. The PR server log confirms `module_causal_conv1d_fwd_split_qkv` was built and invoked by the 9020-token probe.

The previously reported `1.163x` is **operator latency speedup**, not TTFT, TPOT, or model throughput: for the Qwen3.5-35B-A3B TP4 per-rank shape (`D=2048`, BF16, width 4, T=8192), existing Triton conv + fused postprocess measured 0.1375 ms and AITER channel-last split-QKV + fused in-place postprocess measured 0.1182 ms.

title: [XPU][MLA] Support FlashAttnMLA backend on XPU
body:
## Summary

- Route XPU MLA through the existing `FLASH_ATTN_MLA` backend, matching the way XPU support is integrated under `FLASH_ATTN`.
- On XPU, use `vllm-xpu-kernels` `flash_attn_varlen_func` for MLA paged decode by packing `q = [q_nope, q_pe]` and using the latent cache as K with a narrowed V view.
- Keep CUDA FlashAttnMLA behavior unchanged, including FA3 decode/LSE handling.
- Fix XPU varlen output allocation so omitted `out` tensors use the V head dimension. This is required for MLA where Q/K dim is 576 and V dim is 512, and is behavior-preserving for regular attention where `q.shape[-1] == v.shape[-1]`.

## Validation method

Run from a vLLM checkout on an Intel XPU machine with `vllm-xpu-kernels` installed or on `PYTHONPATH`.

1. Unit tests

Run the following ut repeatedly on XPU:
```bash
cd vllm && python3 -m pytest tests/v1/attention/test_mla_backends.py -v
```
Result (on the rebased branch, against latest upstream/main):

```bash
tests/v1/attention/test_mla_backends.py::test_backend_correctness[...] PASSED
... (197 test cases total)
tests/v1/attention/test_mla_backends.py::test_chunked_context_backend_correctness[fp8-glm-MLAPrefillBackendEnum.FLASH_ATTN] PASSED [100%]

=========== 197 passed, 2 skipped, 17 warnings in 190.83s (0:03:10) ===========
```
(The 2 skips are CUDA-only DCP tests, unrelated to XPU.)

2. End-to-end test

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

tmp_script="$(mktemp /tmp/vllm_xpu_mla_validate.XXXXXX.py)"
trap 'rm -f "${tmp_script}"' EXIT

cat >"${tmp_script}" <<'PY'
from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams

def main():
    llm = LLM(
        model="deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V2-Lite",
        tensor_parallel_size=2,
        dtype="bfloat16",
        attention_backend="FLASH_ATTN_MLA",
        block_size=64,
        max_model_len=512,
        trust_remote_code=True,
        enforce_eager=True,
        gpu_memory_utilization=0.80,
    )

    prompts = [
        "Hello, my name is",
        "The capital of France is",
        "The future of AI in 2030 will be",
    ]
    sampling_params = SamplingParams(
        temperature=0.0,
        max_tokens=64,
        repetition_penalty=1.1,
    )
    outputs = llm.generate(prompts, sampling_params)
    for output in outputs:
        print("=" * 60)
        print("PROMPT:", output.prompt)
        print("OUTPUT:", output.outputs[0].text)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
PY

python "${tmp_script}"
```

Expected result:
- Logs show `Using Flash Attention MLA backend on XPU.`
- Generation reaches `Processed prompts: 100%` and prints outputs for all prompts.

This was validated locally on 2x Intel Arc Pro B60; the run logged `Using Flash Attention MLA backend on XPU.`, completed `Processed prompts: 100%`, and generated coherent outputs for all three prompts (e.g. "Hello, my name is" -> "John. I am a 20 year old male...", "The capital of France is" -> "Paris.").

3. Compile check

```bash
python -m py_compile vllm/_xpu_ops.py vllm/platforms/xpu.py vllm/v1/attention/backends/fa_utils.py vllm/v1/attention/backends/mla/flashattn_mla.py vllm/v1/attention/backends/registry.py
```
All 5 changed files compile cleanly with no errors.

4. Accuracy

Ran `lm_eval` with `--model vllm` against DeepSeek-V2-Lite on Intel Arc Pro B60 with `attention_backend=FLASH_ATTN_MLA`:

- TP=2, `dtype=bfloat16`, `max_model_len=4096`, `enforce_eager=True`:
  - GSM8K (5-shot): `exact_match,strict-match` = 0.3723, `exact_match,flexible-extract` = 0.3783
  - MMLU: overall `acc` = 0.5895 ± 0.0277 (humanities 0.5846, other 0.5538, social_sciences 0.7667, stem 0.5053)
- DeepSeek-V2-Lite GSM8K with `ATTENTION_BACKEND=FLASH_ATTN_MLA`, TP=4, `APPLY_CHAT_TEMPLATE=0`, `NUM_FEWSHOT=5`, `MAX_MODEL_LEN=2048` completed successfully; 300-sample result was strict-match 0.3800 / flexible-extract 0.3833, consistent with the base model's expected GSM8K range.

Both are consistent with DeepSeek-V2-Lite's published reference numbers.

title: [Bugfix][PP][Spec Decode] MiniMax-M3 EAGLE3 aux-state relay at PP > 1 and per-stage FlashInfer autotune
body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

Enables EAGLE3 for MiniMax-M3 (NVIDIA model file) at PP > 1 on Model Runner V2, and scopes FlashInfer autotune to each PP stage's TP group, fixing a startup deadlock. Builds on #50514 (PP aux-state relay), changes the autotune sync from #50892, supersedes #57198.

Motivation: MiniMax-M3-NVFP4 PP2/TP4 + EAGLE3 serving on 8x RTX PRO 6000 (also needs #47665). No performance claim; the speedup there comes from split-K admission (#45450 / #52879 / #56148).

## Claims

1. **MiniMax-M3 + EAGLE3 runs at PP > 1.** Base rejects it at load (`ValueError: ... does not support eagle3 with pipeline parallelism`). The drafter then gets all aux states every step; acceptance length and GSM8K match TP8.
2. **FlashInfer autotune no longer deadlocks at PP > 1** when stages tune different shapes. Each stage tunes within its TP group and writes `<cache>_tp_<ranks>.json`. PP = 1 is unchanged.

## Validation

**Setup:** 8x RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (SM120), `nvidia/MiniMax-M3-NVFP4` + `Inferact/MiniMax-M3-EAGLE3`, offline `LLM`, greedy, cold autotune. Both arms: vLLM 213c379 + FP8 Triton-indexer enablement (as in #47665; needed on SM120) + #56148's Triton-attention guard hunks (not its split-K path). Arms differ only in this PR's files as of 4683f1e3 (since then: `kernel_warmup.py` comments only; extractor hunk dropped).

| Config | Aux relay (steps) | Mean AL | GSM8K-200 spec / no-spec | Stage cache entries |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TP8 | – | 3.471 | 94.5 / 94.5 | unchanged |
| PP2/TP4 | 4600/4600 | 3.460, 3.449, 3.452 | 95.5 / 95.5 | 140 / 80 |
| PP3/TP2 | 7200/7200 | 3.469 | 94.0 / – | 140 / 80 / 80 |
| PP4/TP1 | 9200/9200 | 3.498 | 94.0 / – | 140 / 80 / 80 / 80 |

AL: 32 GSM8K prompts × 256 tokens. GSM8K-200: first 200 test questions, chat, thinking on, 0-shot, max 2048 tokens; all within ~1 SE. Autotune ≤10 s/stage.

Main engine args (PP2/TP4):
```text
-tp 4 -pp 2 --attention-backend TRITON_ATTN --attention-config '{"indexer_kv_dtype":"fp8"}'
--kv-cache-dtype fp8 --moe-backend marlin --max-model-len 65536 --language-model-only
--max-num-batched-tokens 4096 --max-num-seqs 12 --block-size 128 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.95
--disable-custom-all-reduce --enable-prefix-caching --seed 0
--speculative-config '{"method":"eagle3","model":"Inferact/MiniMax-M3-EAGLE3","num_speculative_tokens":3,
  "draft_tensor_parallel_size":4,"attention_backend":"TRITON_ATTN","use_local_argmax_reduction":true}'
```

**Base** (same image, base files):
- With these args: the `ValueError` on all 8 ranks.
- Without `--speculative-config`: hangs in autotune; `--kernel-config '{"enable_flashinfer_autotune": false}'` avoids it. PR `model.py` with base `kernel_warmup.py` + EAGLE3 hangs too (both changes needed).
- Non-spec PP2/TP4 (autotune off, 16 prompts, two setups): identical greedy outputs 2–3/16 PR vs base, 2–5/16 PR vs PR (mean hidden cosine .95–.97): no detectable PR effect.

**Non-MiniMax, H200:** Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 bf16 PP2/TP2, PR vs base: both start; PR writes per-stage caches; GSM8K-200 96.0 vs 95.5 (default MoE, 0 tuned entries), 95.5 vs 94.0 (`flashinfer_cutlass`, 44 entries/stage): equivalent.

**Pre-existing, not fixed here:** a warm restart with a `flashinfer_cutlass` cache at PP2/TP2 hangs in base and PR (TP rank 0 hits the cache, rank 1 re-tunes); matches #57423 (fixes: #57579, #57635; untested).

@SloptimistPrime reported the autotune fix on 6x GB10 (SM121), TP2/PP3 (#57198); their test commit 1291f3fe is not included.

**CPU tests and lint:**
```bash
pytest -q tests/model_executor/test_flashinfer_autotune_warmup.py \
  tests/v1/worker/test_eagle3_aux_hidden_states_pp.py
# 17 passed (11 added). Production files reverted: 8 of the 11 fail
# (incl. PP = 1 layer-0 tap); the 3 passing are PP = 1 / no-aux guards.
pre-commit run --hook-stage manual --files $(git diff --name-only 5c3b61e9)
# all pass, incl. mypy 3.10-3.13 and test tethering
```

## Details

**Root cause, autotune.** Since #50892 all ranks sync over the world group (cache broadcast, barrier, per-tactic all-reduce). PP stages can tune different shapes (140 vs 80 `mxfp8_gemm` entries), so PP0 waits on a collective PP1 never joins. Fix: at PP > 1, leader, broadcast, barrier, timing average and cache file use the stage's TP group.

**Root cause, MiniMax-M3.** No #50514 opt-in; taps used stage-local layer indices. Fix: set `supports_aux_hidden_states_over_pp` and use the `EagleModelMixin` helpers (global indices, pack local / collect upstream taps), like Llama, Qwen2, DeepSeek-V4, Kimi-K3. Tap 0 aliases `residual`, which fused add-RMSNorm updates in place, so it is cloned when layer 0 is a tap (any PP size; CPU-tested; GPU runs above use taps 2/30/57).

**Dropped:** #57290's `extract_hidden_states` draft PP = 1 hunk (extractor-only; EAGLE3 unaffected): at PP2 it turned a config-time `NotImplementedError` into a startup `AssertionError` (`ExampleHiddenStatesConnector` needs a change; separate PR). Supersedes earlier status comments.

**Size and tradeoffs.** 2 production files, +40/−13. Tests +342/−2 (CPU fakes). At PP > 1, old unsuffixed caches are not read (one re-tune) and stages may pick different tactics for the same shape (unmeasured). Each PP hop carries one extra `[tokens, hidden]` tensor per upstream tap (not benchmarked).

**Limits.** Aux relay is V2-only (V1: #45985); the autotune change also affects V1 (not run). Untested: MiniMax-M3 dflash/dspark and multimodal inputs at PP > 1 (both now accepted), ROCm (AMD model file unchanged), DP > 1 with PP > 1, MiniMax-M3 FlashInfer MoE (runs used Marlin). CI gap: `test_eagle3_aux_hidden_states_pp.py` does not run on `vllm/models/`-only changes. #57579, #57635, #55671, #52292 also edit `flashinfer_autotune` (on conflict, keep the per-stage group); #53901 reworks the PP aux helpers. No duplicate found.

**AI assistance.** OpenAI Codex, Claude Code and Cursor agents wrote code and tests, ran and analyzed GPU validation, and drafted this text (`/pr-checklist` from unmerged #57084). The human submitter remains responsible for reviewing and defending every changed line.

title: [Bugfix] Preserve GDN recurrent state on zero-draft speculative decode steps
body:
## Purpose

Fix V2 GDN recurrent-state routing when a speculative decode step has zero draft tokens. The current classification can send that step through the non-speculative path, which does not use the accepted-token offset of the speculative state layout.

Active decode rows now remain on the speculative path with a zero draft count. Prefill and padding rows remain excluded, and the decode-row classification used by adaptive verification is preserved.

The V2 runtime change is adapted from #56531 by Vadim Gimpelson; it is not an independently invented implementation. This PR adds focused worker and metadata coverage and FP32/BF16 tests of the actual GDN convolution and SSM recurrent state. The earlier V1 changes have been removed from the final diff; their published commits and discussion remain in the PR history.

I utilized AI tools to assist in refining the implementation, executing tests, and analyzing logs.

## Test Plan

- Verify that zero-draft decode rows remain speculative while prefill and padding rows retain the `-1` sentinel, including adaptive-verification scheduling.
- Check GDN metadata and compare FP32/BF16 convolution and SSM recurrent state with the expected accepted-token state.
- Run Qwen3.5-4B with Eagle3 on the V2 model runner, switching from five drafts to zero by batch size, and compare with plain V2 decoding and unmodified `main`.
- Run Ruff lint/format and `git diff --check`.

title: [Bugfix] DeepSeek-V4 renderer: join tool-result text parts with a blank line like the encoder
body:
## Purpose

Clients such as Claude Code / Cursor send tool results as OpenAI content parts (`[{"type": "text", "text": "..."}, ...]`). `chat_utils._parse_chat_message_content` flattens those parts with a single `"\n"` before the chat template runs, because most templates only accept string content for `tool` messages. The DeepSeek-V4 encoder, however, joins text parts of a tool result with a blank line (`"\n\n".join(text_parts)` in `deepseek_v4_encoding.render_message`), so through vLLM the `<tool_result>` block differs from what the reference encoder renders for the same request.

This PR pre-joins list-of-text `tool` results with `"\n\n"` in `DeepseekV4Renderer` (sync and async paths) before `parse_chat_messages`, so the encoder receives the string it would have produced itself. String content is untouched, and tool results that contain non-text parts (e.g. `tool_reference`) keep the structured list exactly as before.

Related: #58280 (this PR addresses the second item under "Related" in that issue; the issue's main point, tools placement, is already handled on `main` by the `Match the Rust renderer` change in `vllm/tokenizers/deepseek_v4.py`).

## Test Plan

New `tests/renderers/test_deepseek_v4.py`:

- `_join_tool_text_parts`: text parts join with a blank line, string content untouched, non-text parts left structured, input not mutated
- `render_messages` / `render_messages_async` with a stub tokenizer: the conversation handed to `apply_chat_template` carries `"line 1\n\nline 2"`

```
pytest tests/renderers/test_deepseek_v4.py tests/renderers/test_kimi_k3.py -q
```

## Test Result

Run on a CPU box against this branch:

```

```

title: [Bugfix] DeepSeek-V4 parser: drop the content/tool separator so parsed turns re-render byte-identically
body:
## Purpose

DeepSeek-V4's chat template renders an assistant turn that carries visible text and a tool call as `{content}\n\n<｜DSML｜tool_calls>...` (`deepseek_v4_encoding.py`, `tc_content += '\n\n' + tool_calls_template...`), and the reference parser shipped with the model treats that `\n\n` as part of the tool-call opener (`tool_calls_start_token = "\n\n<｜DSML｜tool_calls"` in the model repo's `encoding_dsv4.py`), so the parsed `content` never contains it.

vLLM's `DeepSeekV4Parser` runs with `strip_content_whitespace_with_tools=False` and cuts content at `<｜DSML｜tool_calls>`, so the client receives `"Let me check.\n\n"` as `message.content`. When the client echoes that turn back as history (every agent loop does), the encoder appends its own `\n\n`, and the turn re-renders as `Let me check.\n\n\n\n<｜DSML｜tool_calls>`: four newlines where the model generated two. Every text-then-tool-call turn in a multi-turn agent conversation therefore drifts from the bytes the model produced.

This PR adds an opt-in `content_tool_separator` to `ParserEngineConfig` and sets it to `"\n\n"` for DeepSeek-V4 (V4.1 inherits the config):

- Non-streaming: exactly one trailing separator is removed from `content` when a tool call follows. Nothing else changes (`"text\n"` stays `"text\n"`, `"text\n\n\n"` becomes `"text\n"`, content without a tool call keeps its trailing whitespace).
- Streaming: a trailing (partial) separator is withheld until the engine knows whether a tool block follows; it is dropped when one does and released unchanged when more text arrives or the turn ends without a tool call (`finish_streaming`).

`strip_content_whitespace_with_tools=True` parsers are unaffected (the separator strip runs before their `.strip()`); parsers that do not set the option are unaffected.

Related: #58280 (this PR addresses the first item under "Related" in that issue; the issue's main point, tools placement, is already handled on `main` by the `Match the Rust renderer` change in `vllm/tokenizers/deepseek_v4.py`).

## Test Plan

New tests in `tests/parser/engine/test_deepseek_v4.py::TestContentToolSeparator`:

- non-streaming `extract_tool_calls` / `parse`: exactly one `\n\n` dropped; `\n` and no-separator inputs untouched; no tool call keeps trailing newlines
- streaming: separator in one chunk, split across chunks (`"\n"`,`"\n"`), attached to the opener chunk, and whole turn in one chunk; separator released when text continues or at `finish_streaming`
- round trip: render a history turn with the bundled encoder, take the assistant segment as the model output, parse it, echo the parsed message back, and assert the re-rendered prompt is byte-identical

```
pytest tests/parser -q --ignore=tests/parser/cohere
pytest tests/tool_parsers/test_deepseekv3_tool_parser.py tests/tool_parsers/test_deepseekv31_tool_parser.py tests/tool_parsers/test_deepseekv32_tool_parser.py tests/tool_parsers/test_deepseekv4_tool_parser.py tests/reasoning/test_deepseekv3_reasoning_parser.py -q
```

## Test Result

Run on a CPU box against this branch with the nightly wheel's compiled extensions:

```
tests/parser -q --ignore=tests/parser/cohere        4333 passed (includes the 12 new TestContentToolSeparator cases)
tests/tool_parsers/test_deepseekv4_tool_parser.py    12 passed
```

`tests/parser/cohere` and `tests/parser/mistral` need tokenizers/deps the box cannot fetch, so they were not run locally; CI covers them.

Before this change the new `test_non_streaming_drops_exactly_one_separator[Let me check.\n\n-Let me check.]`, the streaming cases and the round-trip test fail (content is `"Let me check.\n\n"` and the re-rendered prompt has four newlines); after it they pass and the existing tests are unchanged.

title: [Attention][CPU] Run Zen CPU decoder prefill on zentorch SDPA
body:
## Purpose

Route **decoder prefill / extend** on the vLLM CPU backend through `zentorch_sdpa` on Zen CPUs, instead of always using the paged `cpu_attention_with_kv_cache` kernel.

Prefill has no need to gather K/V back out of the page table when the tokens for this step (and, for extends, the already-written cache) can be attended densely. Decode is unchanged: `query_len` at or below the reorder threshold still runs `cpu_attention_with_kv_cache`.

Dispatch:

- **Equal-length fresh prefills** (`query_len == seq_len` for every row): one `zentorch_sdpa.out(is_causal=True)` over a dense `[B, H, S, D]` batch.
- **Ragged fresh prefills and chunked extends**: one padded call with a bottom-right causal mask. Extends gather the cached prefix from the paged K/V cache.
- **Mixed batches**: the metadata builder requests a `[decode | extend | fresh prefill]` order, zentorch fills the prefill suffix, and the native kernel runs only the decode prefix with rebuilt scheduler metadata.

The path is used only for plain decoder self-attention in bf16/fp32 when `zentorch_sdpa` is registered. ALiBi, sliding window, logits softcap, attention sinks, FP8 KV cache, KV-sharing, encoder, and cross-attention stay native. The KV cache write is unchanged (`forward_includes_kv_cache_update = False`); this only skips the paged **read** for prefill rows.

This does not duplicate an in-tree CPU prefill SDPA path. It is the decoder-prefill counterpart of the Zen CPU encoder SDPA work. No `supported_models.md` / examples update: no new model, same CPU backend.

AI assistance was used to implement and review the change. The submitting author reviewed every line.

## Test Plan

On a Zen CPU with zentorch installed (so `torch.ops.zentorch.zentorch_sdpa` is registered):

```bash
# unit tests (skip cleanly on non-Zen / missing op)
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/kernels/attention/test_zen_cpu_prefill_sdpa.py -v

# existing CPU attention suite (decode / mixed / encoder must stay native-correct)
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/kernels/attention/test_cpu_attn.py -v

- Set explicit 30-minute AMD timeouts and include shared evaluation helpers and the selected attention backends in source dependency filters.

Upstream split the former aggregate TurboQuant evaluation into separate format-specific groups. [#50519](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50519), whose history includes [Buildkite AMD CI #12621](https://buildkite.com/vllm/amd-ci/builds/12621), targeted the older aggregate group, so its association needs to be refreshed for the current parents. title: [V1 Scheduler] Fix Priority Queue Preemption Re-admission (#41951)
body:
Fixes #41951

### Context & Root Cause

Under `scheduling_policy="priority"`, `PriorityRequestQueue` delegates queue sorting to `Request.__lt__`. Currently, `Request.__lt__` compares `(priority, arrival_time)`, omitting `num_preemptions`.

When a running request gets preempted and prepended back into `PriorityRequestQueue`, newly arrived requests with earlier timestamps pop ahead of the preempted request. This causes the preempted request to sit waiting while incoming requests overwrite its freed GPU KV cache blocks in VRAM, forcing a full prompt re-computation from scratch upon eventual re-admission.

### Solution

1. Update `Request.sort_key` and `Request.__lt__` in `vllm/v1/request.py` to include a bounded preemption re-admission boost `-min(self.num_preemptions, 3)`:
    ```python
    @property
    def sort_key(self) -> tuple[int, int, float, str, int]:
        return (
            self.priority,
            -min(self.num_preemptions, 3),
            self.arrival_time,
            self.request_id,
            id(self),
        )
    ```
• In Python min-heaps, `num_preemptions=1` evaluates to `-1`, popping preempted requests before fresh requests (`0`) to preserve their KV cache.
• Capping the boost at `3` avoids queue starvation / livelock vulnerabilities for oversized prompts.

2. Align victim preemption selection in `vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py` to protect preempted requests while preserving stable arrival-order tie-breaking.
3. Consolidate unit tests in `tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py` using standard priority fixtures, testing:
   - Priority queue preemption re-admission ordering
   - Preemption boost starvation cap
   - Constrained-capacity victim preemption (least-preempted chosen as victim) and forward progress
   - Equal-arrival-time queue tie-breaking

### Test Plan

• `pytest tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py -k "priority_queue or priority_scheduling_preemption"` (10 passed)
• `pre-commit run --files vllm/v1/request.py vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py` (all passed)
